utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For the appearances, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer; Alexis Demirdjian; legal intern, Ivana Martinovic; and case manager, Indah Susanti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness may be brought in. Mr. Zivanovic, for the planning with regard to the event we spoke about yesterday, how long will you continue your cross-examination today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think until the first break I'll -- I'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Done before the break. Then we will take the first break as late as possible, that means probably at 11.00 unless the Registrar informs me that the records won't hold. 11.00 is okay? At the latest. I know. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Vojnovic. May I remind you that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] good morning, Mr. Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look at the operational diary of your unit, which is Exhibit 557.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have page 6 in the B/C/S and page 10 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is an entry for the 20th of November, 1991, at 0839 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we please zoom in?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we shall certainly do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we need to go a little bit down. 0839 hundred hours. Let us enlarge slightly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see that it is written at 0839 that Colonel Terzic from OG South asked for all the units to withdraw from the Dubrava forest due to the fact that they would be targeted by artillery fire if I read it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My first question is who is Colonel Terzic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Colonel Terzic was at the federal secretariat for national defence at the time and he acted as a kind of support or a monitoring person. His specialty is artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't. He used to be the Chief of Staff at the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear which corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And his first name was Zlatoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Novi Sad Corps in 1995 or 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that his first name was Zlatoje?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that his first name was Zlatoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where this Dubrava forest is located?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. I can't remember. Mitnica, Dubrava, et cetera. I think that but -- no, I wouldn't like to err. But it is within the -- the scope of the area where the road to Sotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what it was necessary on the 20th of November to open artillery fire at the Dubrava forest?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to tell you that. We didn't have any troops there, nor any units. Therefore, I really don't know. I suppose that it came from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at the next entry at 0850.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Colonel, and also for you, Mr. Zivanovic, please respect a pause between questions and answers. The interpreters have difficulty following you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that it says that at 0850 a unit abbreviated to LAD has been notified. Can you tell us what this LAD stands for?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is light artillery battalion. And there is another abbreviation, PVO next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then if I see correctly it is IC?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should mean a reconnaissance company, an acronym.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now can you tell us if this light artillery battalion, is that the same unit that was under the command of Jan Marcek?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say for sure. I know that some elements of these units under Jan Marcek's command were deployed somewhere in the sector of Vucedol.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the name of Jan Marcek's unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Light Artillery Battalion PVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "divizion" is interpreted into English as "battalion" when it deals with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that some elements of that battalion was deployed near Vucedol but this battalion was also under Marcek's command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This battery that was near Vucedol was attached to a unit from the OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to the next page. The date is the 21st of November, 1991. Let us look at the first entry which was made at 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This entry was made at 7.00 in the morning, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And it says that between 0300 and 0400 the positions in Grabovo sector were targeted by infantry fire, that units returned fire, that three shells were fired as well, that there was fire from sniper rifles, and that Lieutenant-Colonel Besovic was notified of the incident. Can you please clarify for us what type of fire was opened between 3.00 and 4.00 in the morning on the 21st of November at Grabovo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember at the moment. Besovic was the commander of the mixed anti-armour artillery battalion. He was a lieutenant-colonel. He's deceased now, unfortunately. He used to be a responsible and conscientious officer. The fire could have come from some of his weapons. But to me it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time on the 21st of November and in those days, was that unit subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm not able to remember because there was a series of resubordination and then units were returned to their original deployment. Therefore, I cannot tell you either way for that specific day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the next entry at 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade has gone to Vukovar and then to Sotin. Did you go to Vukovar and Sotin on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what is written here, it shouldn't be -- or maybe I told them that I would go and therefore they entered it into the log, but I believe that I actually did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember which particular route you took?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a road that leads directly from Negoslavci to Vukovar and then another road from Vukovar to Sotin that runs by the river Vuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you return along the same route; that is to say, via Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I told you there were so many roads that were built, dirt roads that were used by military vehicles, people were always looking for short-cuts or roundabouts; therefore, I cannot claim for sure that I took the same route back. But I definitely didn't travel via Ovcara on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why didn't you given that Ovcara was in your zone of responsibility and you knew what had happened on the day before? Weren't you not interested to see whether there were any prisoners still there, whether there were any troops or units there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday that was in general the area of responsibility of the OG South, and they carried out their activities there. And I'm not aware of any different situation, what happened there. I didn't go there ever. I had heard what transpired there but I don't think that many people went there, particularly my officers from my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the previous day on the 20th of November that you were supposed to meet with Marcek, that Marcek was waiting for you in front of the command building but that did you not stay there; rather, you proceeded following the buses that were heading towards the hangar. What I wanted to ask you is: How did you arrange this meeting with Marcek?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Marcek didn't know that I would be there. I did not call ahead. I simply had some time on my hands when I headed out from Sotin to visit him as well. I wanted to see him. He had deployed his unit there quite recently and I wanted to see how things were working out with his small command to see if he had any problems, and then I wanted to go to Negoslavci to attend a briefing with my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking you this is because I understood you to have said yesterday that Marcek had been waiting for you in front of the command.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Marcek saw the car. He saw me coming from the direction of Sotin and he simply came out and stood in front of the command building because he recognised my car. He didn't know that I would be coming, but he simply waited there to salute me and to submit his report in line with the military protocol. I did not stop there, as I told you yesterday. I went immediately to see about the buses, who was on the bus, who was getting off the buses, why they were there, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, Marcek didn't know that you would be coming. It was only when he saw your car that he went out to give his report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He didn't know that I would be coming because I had not called ahead from Sotin to tell him that I would be passing by. I simply had some spare time and I wanted to take this opportunity to see what he was doing, whether he had any problems, how things were going, and so on, on that day and in general, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. We are done, I think, with the operational diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear you and the court reporter didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D56. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that when you were in the hangar that you saw a person sitting at the desk making a list of prisoners or something like that. We have some indication that a man nicknamed Joca Kafic actually did that. Do you know that person, Joca Kafic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that person. He's from Kragujevac. He was a -- the assistant commander of the LAD PVO, the light battalion for morale. He came from an officer's family and he was very disciplined, conscientious, responsible, spick and span. And I know that he had a cafe in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that he was an officer from the light artillery battalion, was this the unit commanded by Marcek?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look in greater detail in this document that's number 27 on our list. We looked at it yesterday but let's now analyse it. No, it's apparently not 27. Just a moment. I beg your pardon, I -- it appears that it's a different document. Yes, yes. That's the one. It's the notebook. It's the operational notebook, as we called it. Vezmarovic's notebook. He was the military police company commander in your unit. Now let's look at page 33. I think we actually need to see the other side of the page enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise. Just to be clear what we see on the right side of the screen is not a translation of -- of the B/C/S, because we still see the same excerpt that we saw yesterday on the screen, so I don't think the entire diary is translated, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You could see here that we see again SIT, Captain Karanfilov, and we see a list of defenders with Filip Karaula, et cetera. So I don't think this is what you want, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know this is a document from the Rule 65 ter list and it has to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, the Registrar tells me that there are only two pages translated out of 46 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why the whole document was not translated. Really I don't know. As far as I know it was I suppose that the Prosecution did it when they put it under -- on its Rule 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The translation we have here is from the Mrksic case. It was the excerpt that was relevant in that case and that is all that's been translated, Your Honours. So if the Defence wish to use that or parts I think the translation has to be provided at that stage, or at least they have to notify us that they need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, what is your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was -- was put at -- on the list, on our list. And the Prosecution was informed that we shall use this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I mean, it is the party's responsibility to make sure a translation is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would say whatever the cause is, the problem is that we have a B/C/S text that you want to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: While we, I mean the Trial Chamber, doesn't know what it says. And I -- there is no way to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would -- I would show to the witness just for -- four or five lines of this text, and I could read it from -- from this document and it could be translated in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the better course would be for the interpreters to read it. I would rather have the official interpreters translate this into the record, Your Honour, than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- read it from screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if they have that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do they have it on the screen? The Registrar says they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we do have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You do have it on the screen. Mr. Zivanovic, which lines would you like to

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second part, the second part below the numbers -- ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The part that the Registrar zoomed in now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could the interpreters translate it from the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Zivanovic could read it and then we can interpret his words while reading it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We could go along with that. Please, Mr. Zivanovic, if you would read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it's the text that is right below the list of prisoners that you were shown yesterday. And below the list, at the end of the list, we read the following words: "Received on the 18th of November, 1991, at around 1600 hours, at the farm in the village of Ovcara, handed over to Captain Karanfilov on the 19th of November, 1991, at around 11.30. The lists were provided to the Sremska Mitrovica penitentiary penal facility on the 19th of November, 1998, at around 1530." And then we see Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic, Captain Zoric, dash "garda."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday we discussed this list. The captain simply noted this down with the time-line and he wanted to have some record of what he had done and that he had actually handed them over to the officers that are signed there. Well, he couldn't record it anywhere else but in his operational book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you testified yesterday that Vezmarovic took those prisoners who are listed here to the correctional and penal facility in Sremska Mitrovica, yet from this record it would seem that they were handed over to Karanfilov at around 11.30?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was in charge of securing and escorting those prisoners, ensuring their safety. And you can see that Captain Karanfilov was in charge of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you another entry from this notebook at page 35. It's just a single sentence at the bottom part of the page. It says here: "The centre for the provision of care to civilians and property, Commander Ljubinko Stojanovic." Do you know what kind of a centre we are talking about, a centre for the provision of care to civilians and property?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in Velepromet there were some premises where some items were stored, food and other items and some other property that was brought into Vukovar, because assistance was needed to repair those items and also to perhaps make some things operational. But I couldn't really be more specific than that. Civilians who in my opinion - in my opinion - did not have anywhere else to go or did not dare to go to the centre of the town would gather there, the elderly civilians would gather there, all those who were not involved in any units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We don't have to belabour that. Let me just ask you this: Do you know this man, Ljubinko Stojanovic, who he was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the man I'm thinking of, Ljubinko Stojanovic was a man from Vukovar. He organised some cultural activities later on, Radio Vukovar, so he was active in the propaganda efforts in Vukovar together with his men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like you to look at an entry at page 36. It's right at the beginning of the page. There is a name written here, Zavisic, and it says the command of the police station in Vukovar, Miodrag Zavisic. Can you tell me, do you know who that man was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. At page 37, the next page, right at the beginning in the upper left-hand corner you see "no statements for the public, Lieutenant-Colonel Bogdanovic." Do you know who Lieutenant-Colonel Bogdanovic was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several men with the same last name, Bogdanovic, but I know that there was a Lieutenant-Colonel Bogdanovic. His first name was Mile. He was my assistant for morale for a very short time in Vukovar, and I can now tell you why that was, because the press -- the media were really exerting great pressure on everyone asking people to make statements, public statements, and this is probably why he said that, in order to prevent the personnel from making statements and from talking to the media. That's why he made this note.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood that this instruction was issued after the fighting had stopped and I would like to know whether you know why no public statements were made after the fighting stopped?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know how it is. All kinds of comments were made, people were bragging, they were trying to stress their own importance, inaccurate information, and that is indeed the worst part, and I think that is why he did what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us take a look at page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. We started with four lines. Now we're looking at a fifth page. There is no translation again. We are looking at pages written in Cyrillic. We have no idea. We are left in the dark. Once again, I would really insist that if counsel wishes to use something, he has to make sure that the parts that are relevant to his cross-examination are translated. We cannot be expected to translate entire notebooks, diaries, manuals. I think it's counsel's responsibility at this stage to provide us translations and to know what we are looking at on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is exclusive fault of the Prosecution not to translate document from their list. That -- they did not say that they put on the list just one page or two pages but they -- they put the document on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think that is completely wrong, Your Honours. We have manuals on our list. We have -- we have the military lexicon that is 2.000 pages. We cannot expect CLSS or any of our units to translate every page without knowing what the Defence wishes to use. And again, it is the responsibility of counsel who is preparing for his cross-examination to prepare the documents he will display before the Trial Chamber. And again, I believe we are left in the dark. It is really not a useful exercise if we don't have before us the translations that are necessary for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not the document of 2.000 pages but just 49 pages. And just to conclude, I'll just read one name from this book from this particular page, and I'll complete my cross-examination as regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which name would that be -- sorry, which name would that be, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Stricevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what would be the use of reading that name from this document? I mean, there is no context. We know who Stricevic is. If you want to ask something about Colonel Stricevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- we can do it without the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to see whether the witness knows anything about Stricevic and about the contacts between Stricevic and his commander of military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Why don't you just ask it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vojnovic, in this notebook there is mention of Lieutenant-Colonel Stricevic. Do you know who Lieutenant-Colonel Stricevic is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is Lieutenant-Colonel Marko Stricevic. He was the chief of the medical corps in the 80th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now take a look and go through your statement. First of all, let us look at paragraph 13 of your statement number 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 13 begins on page 6 in the B/C/S and continues on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the next page, you spoke about the burial of the dead bodies that were found in Vukovar, and I think it was about 400 dead bodies, and you also made a reference to Colonel Basic from the 1st Military District Command. Can you tell us when this happened? When this burial of dead bodies took place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly when this activity started. But following the liberation of Vukovar and the establishment of the brigade command and its transfer to the barracks in Vukovar, Colonel Basic came to see me every afternoon seeking assistance in troops and in motor vehicles in order to help him with the identification of the bodies and their burials. That was somewhere in the region of the Turkish cemetery as it was called in Vukovar. He really did that in the most conscientious and responsible way. He marked every body, he put a cross, he wrote the name whenever he knew that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We know all about that. You needn't repeat it. In paragraph 20 you speak about the investigations and the participation of the military police in them, and there is mention of the case of the three men from Leva Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at Exhibit 1D361.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the wounding of the commander of the TO Vukovar. I think you were the one who compiled it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the bottom of the B/C/S document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I see that you authored this report and it says at the very end that: "The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the wounding of Vujovic is underway and you will be informed it in due course." Can you tell me what was the follow-up procedure and what was done in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this procedure was carried out by security organs. It was established, the identity of the person who wounded Vujovic was established, and how this accident happened. And there is a description of the whole event, nothing else. I suppose that the superior command was informed about this as well and you see that this is addressed to the 1st Military District Command. Whether there was any subsequent forensic report, I'm not aware of that, but it actually happened as described here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zivanovic please repeat his question. There was an overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I repeat my question. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not disputing the contents of this document, but my question was whether there was any follow-up report because this is what is being indicated in the last sentence of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you if anything special was done except that this went to the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will tender this document into evidence. I'll repeat. I would tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit D57. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have document 1D364.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 25 of your statement, you speak about what the responsibilities of the town command were. This is yet another document produced, I believe, on the 16th of November. Can you please clarify for me item 2 of this order that you issued. It reads that in Sotin authorities should be organised: "... pursuant to the rules of service -- of service and the proper provision relating to service in garrison and barracks and to take all necessary measures to prevent the infiltration of sabotage and terrorist groups and carrying out of terrorist acts, draft instruction for work and ensure a normal living and working conditions for the population and prevent any ill-treatment of the local population and unauthorised entry and search of flats and houses." Those were within the scope of the responsibilities of town commands, everything that I read out to you and everything that is contained in paragraph 2 of this order.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was specifically relevant for the village of Sotin because that was the largest village of that type where our units were deployed, and as a result it was possible to organise normal life because it did not sustain so much damage like other places and it could provide better living conditions. And for that reason, the logistics battalion was deployed as well because the conditions were good and supplies were possible for all brigade units, particularly in terms of quartermaster and technical support. There were also workshops. There was a clinic which served both the brigade and the entire population living in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document 6029.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated the 20th of November, 1991, and it deals with the appointment of Jan Marcek, commander of Ovcara. As far as I can see, your order under item number 2 is identical to the previous one. You said that Sotin was a specific place but I can see that you issued identical order with respect to Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a universal order. Ovcara only had this one facility. There was no civilian population as was the case in Sotin, and that is why I put the emphasis on Sotin, although the whole arrangement was identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the command -- the town command responsibilities were the same; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender these two documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is -- this last document is a duplicate. We've already admitted a document with the same content. I can check the exhibit number, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, do you have an exhibit number already for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please give an exhibit number to the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D364 shall be assigned Exhibit D58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record, it was tab 12 in the Prosecution list, and this order on the 20th of November - yes - it was part of the package which was admitted yesterday. It was at tab 12. It was 65 ter 633, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zivanovic, you agree we do not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- need to admit a duplicate?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: A duplicate is not necessary, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was assigned Exhibit P1991.1981. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you spoke about paragraph 26, you were shown a document that pertains to Ilok, and it says that there was dissatisfaction with how the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was operating. At that time, did you have any contacts with the Ilok command? Did you co-operate with them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no contacts and I did not co-operate with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a word, you saw this document for the first time when the Prosecution showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 27, it reads and you mentioned Radovan Stojicic, aka Badza, and it says here that you thought that he was the TO commander but later on it turned out that that was not the case. Can you remember when did you find out that he was not the TO commander? Was that after the fighting in Vukovar, let's say in December, January, until the end of your term, or was it before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure that it happened after the fighting in Vukovar because it was possible for me to reach Dalj, and I saw the house where he was billeted, but I didn't find anyone there. I wanted to get in touch with him but I failed in doing so, and I never saw him either then or later. But I did hear later what he turned out to be and what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean "what he turned out to be"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether that was the same person who later became a high-ranking police official. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 28, you state that Colonel Mrksic, as he was at the time, the commander of the OG South, ordered an inspection of the volunteers and local TO and ordered that they had to be integrated into a single detachment - so I'm reading from your statement, paragraph 28 - and it is after that the 1st Vukovar Detachment was formed. Was this inspection of the volunteers and the TO ever carried out as ordered by Colonel Mrksic, or rather, was it carried out while he was still there or at a later date?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Mrksic ordered that this volunteer detachment be set up, prepared, I don't know the exact strength, and that all of them should become part of my unit and be subordinated to me. All the troops and the equipment. This was never carried out. But when I assumed the command of the town and when Colonel Mrksic left for Belgrade, we established a TO detachment, the 1st TO Vukovar Detachment, and a large part of those volunteers who were Seselj's men, and so on, joined this detachment. They were lined up, armed, equipped, for once they looked like a real army, real soldiers, and then they were disbanded. They were demobilised after they were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 53 of your statement. In this paragraph - we are about to see it on our screens, in Serbian as well - you say that Captain Vezmarovic issued an order to withdraw security only after Captain Karanfilov's announcement that the detainees were being handed over to the TO. Could you please tell me whether you learned that from Vezmarovic or were you there in person while this was going on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not there in person. Vezmarovic reported to me when he came here and I also heard the same report from Captain Marcek, the artillery battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to Karanfilov at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I saw him but I did not speak to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you ask him about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why would I? He was in charge of those prisoners providing security to them. We didn't know that. And he actually went public, as Vezmarovic told me, and he said that the JNA units were not under any kind of obligation vis-a-vis the Territorial Defence, that they should surrender to the Territorial Defence units, and that the SAO Krajina government had been established with the judiciary and the police force and that they would be in charge of the proceedings from then on. It was very clear, unequivocal. He stated in no uncertain terms that he did not have any obligations in that case, and it was only after that that Vezmarovic came back and reported to me, as did Captain Marcek.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to clear this up. He -- you said that he went public, what does it mean? Did he talk to the media?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Marcek told me. I don't know how it happened, whether he came to the command post or what, in Negoslavci, I mean. And he said that the Territorial Defence was taking over the prisoners. I -- he went after the police and he came there to tell me that the police had packed up their bags and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clear this up, what you just said. Let me read in English what is stated in the transcript: "[In English] And he actually went public, as Vezmarovic told me, and he said that the JNA units were not under any kind of obligation vis-a-vis the Territorial Defence ..." [Interpretation] I won't be reading any further, but could you please tell me how did Vezmarovic tell you that this was made public? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he stood in front of the prisoners and the Territorial Defence members and there were also troops from my unit, and he said the prisoners who are here are now taken over by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat what he said. So when you say that he went public, that means that he said it out loud in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, please don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 61 you speak about a meeting held on the eve of the Guards Brigade's departure. You attended this meeting, as did Major Sljivancanin, and Vujovic and Vujanovic. Could you tell me, please, how did you come to be at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really tell you why I happened to be at that meeting. The meeting was held at Velepromet. I don't know if somebody told me about it, whether I received a report to that effect. But I really was there. Sljivancanin was there. It was in a room where 30 or 40 people could fit in. He said that the Guards Brigade was leaving Vukovar and that it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, don't repeat what you had already said. Could you please limit your answer to my question. My question was how you came to be there, so I didn't ask you about what the participants said because you have already testified about that and I don't want your testimony to be repetitive. My question is: Was that the first time after the 20th of November that you saw Vujovic and Vujanovic in person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not seen them before. I think that was the first time that I saw them after the event, when I saw them at Velepromet. I think they were there because you could not hold a meeting of that kind in their absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you think they were there, but in your statement in paragraph 61 you say that you were introduced to Vujovic and Vujanovic and to all the others who were present there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were there but I can't really tell you with any certainty. But what I can tell you for sure is that this meeting could not have been held without them. Sljivancanin introduced me to all of them, not only to Vujovic and Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when was the first time that you saw Vujovic and Vujanovic after the events at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not seem them for sure. I think I may have seen them at the end of November. As I said, they did not come to the command all that often, and it's really a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a word, you cannot be specific about when you saw them after the event at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot be specific about the time when I saw them first after the events at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 68 you say that the events at Ovcara were not spoken about at the briefings of OG South. And yet in paragraph 69 I can see that you say that Mrksic issued an order to prepare the accommodation of a team of investigators coming to look into what happened at Ovcara. So was this order issued outside of the meeting or in some other context?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events at Ovcara were not mentioned at the meetings and perhaps it was at this meeting or some subsequent meeting, but Mrksic did say that premises should be made ready for the team of investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You reported to your officers about the events at Ovcara or, rather, as you say in paragraph 69 you heard about what had happened the night before. You informed your officers, and you said that things like that should not happen again. I want to ask you this: After you heard what happened the night before at Ovcara - in other words, that the prisoners had been executed - did you raise this issue with Mrksic since Ovcara was in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did gather up my command, members of my command, and I told them what happened, and I warned them that such incidents should not and could not happen again. I also discussed some other things. And I couldn't report to Mrksic because he was in charge of that and he was much more aware of the situation. He knew more about the situation than I did since he was the commander of OG South. He had the powers to organise a team of investigators, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you did not understand my question. But you heard about what happened at Ovcara the night before, that the prisoners who had been abused were later executed, so did you report to Mrksic about what you had heard?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I knew that Mrksic knew more than I did about the situation. I did report what I knew. I said, as I already said, this was not discussed in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your area of responsibility stretched along just one bank of the river Vuka and that on the other side of the river another unit, I think it was the Novi Sad Corps, was in charge. It was its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you a document. It's the Prosecutor's document and the number is 1684.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So P1684.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the context of those numerous volunteer units that were present in the area covered by OG South and in, indeed, your area of responsibility, do you know if Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's unit, was present in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not in my unit. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at this report issued by the 16th Corps command from December, 1991, and I would like you to look --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 2 in the English version. I want to see paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see in paragraph 8 there is a list of volunteer units that were part of the 12th Corps. It's the Novi Sad Corps, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the last one is Arkan's unit. I think this is the Territorial Defence detachment, volunteer Territorial Defence detachment with 70 conscripts. Now I want to ask you if you know that at that time Arkan's unit was present in the area of responsibility of the 12th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where this unit was deployed. I saw Arkan with the corps commander, General Biorcevic, about two or three times, and based on that I concluded that he was there. I also heard about his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you are a career officer, how do you read the first sentence in paragraph 8: "The following volunteer units belong to the ranks of the 12th Corps:" Do you read this as meaning that those units were subordinated to the 12th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can interpret it both ways. It means that they could be acting in concert with those units, that they were present in the area of responsibility, or indeed that they were subordinated to the 12th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the team of investigators that arrived in the area and that you knew about it, and I want to know -- well, you said that you knew about Major Stankovic. Let me remind you, you testified before the war crimes court in Belgrade -- or rather, I didn't mean to ask you that. You testified in the Vukovar case on the 15th of May, 2006, before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Exhibit 4628.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you this: You state here that you saw -- well, I can find the exact page in the transcript. You say that you did not see those investigators in person, just some of them, and that you say that Colonel Papic was there, he was a prosecutor at the time, but that you did not know any of the others. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him before that, not in that capacity, but he attended the meeting with Mrksic and then he was introduced to me as Prosecutor Colonel Papic. I did not see him after that. And I even heard that he came originally from the village of Negoslavci. If that's true or not, I cannot really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was there at the time while Colonel Mrksic was still in Vukovar -- or, rather, Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this same transcript I think on page 58 you explained the composition of your unit. You mentioned the 1st Battalion, and you said, among other things, that a Major Susa was the commander of that battalion and that his deputy was a Captain Dusko Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me first whether his proper name was Dusko or Dusan?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that his proper name is Dusan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that on that occasion you said that they were resubordinated to some other unit in the OG North.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know where they were; for example, where Filipovic was? Was he in the area of OG North in Serbia or in this part of Yugoslavia around Sid?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the area of OG North, commanded by the 12th Corps. I know that they had been detached to the village of Klisa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they leave before or after you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the first unit that left and that was on the 29th of October, 1991, and they departed from Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in the aftermath of these events and with regard to Ovcara events, in particular, did you conduct any conversations with people who were involved in all of that in some sort of way with people who had certain roles either in the hangar or at Velepromet or at Grabovo and at other places?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that this issue was never discussed. I never heard anyone discussing it either in the command of OG South or in my command. Whether there were any private conversations about that, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, I have quite a lot of information about this meeting in Velepromet. And according to the information that I have, a JNA officer attended the meeting, he introduced himself as the commander of the town of Vukovar. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the meeting. I don't know who else was there, but I did not introduce myself because I was not the town commander yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I have, your name, your rank, and your post were all listed there among the attendees. Were there any other Milorad Vojnovic's there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know if there were any Milorad Vojnovics who are officers, military officers, I don't know about that. There are Vojnovics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just say one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the statements and the allegation that I did not mention any names in either of the statements, the first trial in the Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic case confirmed that I was there and that I mentioned those names. I said that Vukasinovic was there, Panic, and Karanfilov, and all the others. Marcek, Vezmarovic, Vukosavljevic, Vukic, Vukasinovic himself, they can all confirm, and Vukasinovic did confirm that in the Seselj trial, he said that he had been there and that he had thought that the Territorial Defence would take over the prisoners and would try them, prosecute them, and so on. So all those men can confirm what I have just said. I mentioned all those names and I don't know why that was not recorded. That's all I wanted to say. And there are probably some other people who can confirm that I said all along that those people had been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Demirdjian, how long will you have for redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, depending on the answers approximately 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take the break now. Let's keep it on the safe side and say that we come back at 11.45. Mr. Vojnovic, the Court Usher will escort you out of court for our second break that will last for 45 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And may the record reflect that Mr. Stringer had to leave during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I just have a few questions to clarify some of the answers you gave during cross-examination this morning. Now, do you remember this morning that Mr. Zivanovic asked you about the entries in the operation -- operations diary of your brigade, especially the one on the 20th of November which refers to Colonel Terzic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you ask me about that? I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. This morning Mr. Zivanovic asked you about an entry in the diary of your brigade, and there is a mention of a Colonel Terzic. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Mr. Zivanovic asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that you answered and said that the full name of this Colonel was Zlatoje Terzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you also told us that he was a member of the SNNO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I cannot tell you exactly whether he was from the SSNO or from the General Staff, but I think he was from the Federal Secret of National Defence, SSNO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a document on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It is 65 ter 6389, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I haven't had the opportunity to show you this document before, so if you'd like to take a moment to take a look at it. You'll see that it's from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence on the 29th of September, 1991. Are you able to read what's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the section below "I hereby order ..."?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the names here of Nebojsa Pavkovic and Zlatoje Terzic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And after their name it says that both are from the office of the SSNO; is that right? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now generally speaking, are you aware -- were you aware at the time that Pavkovic and Terzic had been sent from Belgrade to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I saw Pavkovic once and as for Terzic I saw him once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And are you familiar with the person who signs the document, Vuk Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Should be assigned Exhibit P2011. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now earlier this morning, and for the record this was at page 42, Mr. Zivanovic asked you a question which related to this meeting at Velepromet which you learnt about later on, so after the events in Vukovar. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember being at Velepromet and that was prior to the departure of the Guards Brigade from Belgrade. One or two days before, Major Sljivancanin was the main speaker there saying that the people are leaving, that everything is order -- in order now, and that the 80th Brigade was replacing the Guards Brigade and assuming their duties, and that somebody from the 80th Brigade would be appointed town commander. There were no other major issues, but I realise that Sljivancanin was quite familiar with the people there and they were familiar with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that clarification. Now, this is what I'd like to ask you: Mr. Zivanovic was referring to paragraph 62 and 63 of your statement when he asked you those questions and those paragraphs deal with a meeting in Velepromet on the 20th of November, and it was a meeting where the JNA and the government of the SAO SBWZ were present. And in response to one of his questions you said: "I attended the meeting. I don't know who else was there but I did not introduce myself because I was not the town commander yet." So can I ask you to clarify, when you say "I attended the meeting," which meeting are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the meeting held at Velepromet and where Sljivancanin spoke before the brigade left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you just told us a minute ago this was a few days before they left for Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be 100 per cent sure. A couple of days before they left for Belgrade, that's when the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now the last topic that I would like to deal with is the statements in 1998 that you gave and which were admitted earlier this morning. Now, the first one that was admitted was Exhibit D59.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I would like us to display that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And while it's coming up, you told us before the break that these are -- well, let me get the exact excerpt here. You explained at page 43 of the transcript -- well, you explained your position, basically, and you say here that you did mention all those names and you did not know why they were not recorded. You remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I still cannot believe that this was not recorded. As for the statement that I gave to Colonel Gajic, I learned about that here in The Hague. And as for the statement taken by Radomir Gojovic is something that I've seen for the first time here and I was not aware that he omitted to include that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now if we look at the first paragraph of the document that we have in front of us, do you see the initial sentence which reads: "Authorised officials of the security organ of Military Post 9922 Belgrade ..." Now first of all, I will stop here for a second. Do you know what this military post 9922 is? What does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which military posts in Belgrade that is, but I suppose that it's the military post, the peacetime military post of the Guards Brigade in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The sentence continues: "... acting upon request of the military prosecutor in Belgrade, KR no.3/98 of 12 January, 1998, to collect necessary information relating to the indictment issued by the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia against Veselin Sljivancanin, Mile Mrksic, and Miroslav Radic, for several crimes comitted against civilian population and prisoners of war," et cetera. Now at the time when you were interviewed, were you informed of the context within which you were giving this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I was told was that it deals with the events and that relates to the proceedings instituted against Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin in relation to the Ovcara events. That's what I've been told. They used to call them the "Vukovar trojka."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now I know it's been several times, but do you remember at the time or did you know when the indictment was issued against Mrksic, Sljivancanin and Radic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, as part of these proceedings, are you aware as to whether you were the only one interviewed or were there other witnesses interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I was interviewed and as for my unit I think that Dragi Vukosavljevic, the security organ, was also interviewed, as well as the police company commander, Vezmarovic, Jan Marcek. Now I remember another one, Svetolik Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. For this purpose you don't have to name everyone. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean I didn't see it. I don't know when or where it happened. But I presume that it did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you aware as to whether members of the Guards Brigade were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Vukasinovic was interviewed at the same time when I was interviewed by the investigating judge. I was interviewed first. We said hello to one another, and I think that on that occasion as well I had seen him standing in the hangar. So as I say, I saw him on that occasion and we talked. Of course, I heard that interviews were conducted with Sljivancanin and with others, but as for this one I am quite sure. Yes, no, I'm sorry. Miodrag Panic was with me in Belgrade when we were interviewed by the investigating judge and he was from the brigade as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this morning at pages 37, 38, you told us that the investigating judge told you your statement is fair but you're neglecting one thing. There are defending Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic. Now you added that you did not know who he was referring to when he said "they are defending." I'd like to return to that answer of yours. How was this information conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after I finished inside my statement - and I should add that I knew Gojovic from before in Sarajevo where he was a commander and I knew that he had become a judge in the meantime - after reading my statement he said, "You gave a fair statement but you overlooked the fact that the people you are talking to are the ones who are defending Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin," and those were, in fact, attorneys at law. Now I remember their names, Mr. Vasic, Mr. Lukic. I only know their last names. And whether Borovic or Borovjevic, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And now you say that the people you are talking to are the ones who are defending Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin. I'm not entirely clear. Were you taking to them? Were they present during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I talked very briefly with Mr. Lukic and Mr. Vasic. Now as for Borovic or Borovjevic, I didn't talk to him at all. That was not a meeting where minutes were taken. We were just sitting together in an informal fashion. I used -- to tell them a few things and that's how it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know how Gojovic was aware that you had spoken to Vasic, Lukic, and Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once Gojovic and Lukic came to Backa Palanka to meet with me and to talk to me. And I also saw Lukic at the special court in Belgrade. We exchanged a few words, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And with respect to these two statements this morning you told us, and this is at page 39, that "my words were not recorded properly." Do you stand behind these two statements?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by these two statements 1 million per cent, not 100 per cent. Because that's what I said. If I omitted to say that and that was a key thing, I would have assumed the responsibility for which I cannot be held responsible, and I mention that in my previous statement, that they were there, and this is repeated throughout all my subsequent statements. Now this statement made by the investigating judge which I'd never seen before, and Gajic is one I did see earlier and I reacted immediately. And each and every statement was corrected in that respect and it was confirmed that that was the case; i.e., that Vukasinovic, Karanfilov, and Panic and the assistants for morale were indeed in the hangar. But I don't see their names here. I don't know why. Probably I was too relaxed and I honestly believed that they would sincerely record and faithfully record what I was saying, but it seems to me that their intention was to try and to protect someone from what I might possibly say and that turned out to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is all the questions I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would put some questions arising from the redirect to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, did anything new arise from the redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing new. Just as to clarification of his statement from the page 41, 42, as told by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Just a few questions then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vojnovic, a question was asked at page 41 of today's transcript about your statement, paragraphs 62 and 63 of your statement. You have an opportunity to look at those paragraphs on your screen. We were talking about the meeting at Velepromet where a decision was made what to do about the prisoners. This is what I specifically stressed. And I asked you when you heard about that for the first time, and you said that General Panic told you that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you when you heard for the first time about the meeting at Velepromet when the decision was made to hand over the prisoners. Let me just -- yes, just a moment. Let me finish my question. So I asked you about when you heard that for the first time and you said that General Panic told you that when you were giving a statement to the investigating judge, both of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then I put it to you at page 42 that I have a lot of information about that meeting at Velepromet and that according to the information that I have that meeting was attended by a JNA officer who introduced himself as the town commander. You remember my question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he said that he was the town commander, that that's how he introduced himself? Because the brigade commander and the town commander are two different things. There was the town command. I don't know who that officer may have been. But there was the town command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But as the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said here: "I attended this meeting. I don't know who else was there, but I did not introduce myself because I was not the town commander."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am reading back your answer which was recorded and indeed was transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two terms are confused here, "town command" and "brigade command." There was a separate town command and the brigade command was a separate entity. It was located in the Vukovar barracks. The town command had different tasks, that's what we explained, and it was subordinated to the brigade. Since civilian structure, civilian authorities were supposed to be set up, somebody from the town command probably was present there. I don't know who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put something else to you. According to the information that I have, the officer introduced himself as Milorad Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Perhaps you're mixing things up because I was there when the executive government of Vukovar was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's not go into that. Don't go into that. I'm asking you about an event of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please, gentlemen. One, two, three, four, five. Should I continue? Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, I'm asking you about one event. Please don't talk about other events. So I'm talking to you about the meeting at Velepromet where the purported hand-over of the prisoners was carried out on the 20th of November. I am not interested in any other meeting. So I put it to you that I had information that a JNA officer was present there and that he introduced himself as Milorad Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your information is wrong. I was not there 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us when were you appointed the town commander?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This goes beyond the scope now. We've covered the issue of the meeting sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In course of redirect the witness answered that he was not at the time the commander of town and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So can you tell me when were you appointed the town commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall the exact date. It must have been in December just before the Guards Brigade left. That would be logical. For as long as they were there, they exercised the function of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you appoint other town commanders as the town commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Guards Brigade left, we appointed the commanders in the villages around Vukovar. So they were village commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to look at the document, the operational diary of your unit. We don't have to look at it now. But I saw there that Jan Marcek was appointed the commander of Ovcara on the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that you appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Let me give you a clarification. Jan Marcek was not a part of my unit at the time. But since we knew that the units were leaving and since he was being returned to my unit, I assumed the right to appoint him although I did not have the power. At that time on that day he was still subordinated to the OG South, but I did issue an order appointing him the village commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And until the 19th of November, he was subordinated to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To OG South, the chief of the artillery and anti-aircraft artillery service. I can't remember his name. He was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you issued the order appointing him the village commander, the commander of the village of Ovcara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you why you did that, whether you consulted anyone or not. But you issued the order.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that Marcek was subordinated to this commander that you mention. I think you said that his name was Losanovic [phoen]. You spoke about him earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was in professional terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
